findings.paper_title: Lewisham Council Housing Performance Overview 2025-26 REPORT
findings.headline: PFI-managed housing stock of 1,823 properties returns to council direct management June 2027
findings.detail: Council has 1,223 tenanted and 600 leasehold properties in Brockley and Ladywell wards managed under 20-year PFI contract expiring June 2027. Following contract end, management returns to direct council control. This operational transition occurs in 18 months, bringing ~1,800 homes into direct management while council manages intensive improvement programmes and operational pressures.
findings.matters: Operational transition of 1,800 homes requires capacity investment and planning, creating risk during intensive improvement period
findings.figures: 1,223 tenanted properties; 600 leasehold; PFI contract ending June 2027
findings.quote: at the end of 2025-26, the council had 1,223 tenanted properties and 600 leasehold properties in Brockley and Ladywell wards that are managed under a 20-year Private Finance Initiative (PFI) that will end in June 2027. Post June 2027, the management of these PFI properties will be returning to the council.

findings.paper_title: Lewisham Council Housing Performance Overview 2025-26 REPORT
findings.headline: Tenant satisfaction measures mostly in third or fourth quartiles versus London peers; complaints at 26%
findings.detail: Overall satisfaction with landlord service remained stable at 52% (from 51% prior year), with seven of twelve perception measures recording higher scores. Most satisfaction measures fall in bottom two quartiles against London peers. Satisfaction with complaints handling approach remained at 26%, the lowest-rated measure. This is broadly comparable to London median of 28% but indicates persistent service quality gaps.
findings.matters: Weak service satisfaction across most measures signals operational issues relevant to regulatory compliance and tenant engagement
findings.figures: 52% overall satisfaction (unchanged); 26% complaints handling satisfaction (lowest); most measures in 3rd-4th quartile vs peers
findings.quote: Benchmarking indicates that, with the exception of complaints handling, most satisfaction measures fall within the third or fourth quartiles amongst London peers, highlighting the need for continued improvement in the customer experience.

findings.paper_title: Lewisham Council Housing Performance Overview 2025-26 REPORT
findings.headline: Non-emergency repairs at 66% on time, 20 percentage points below London median of 86%
findings.detail: Emergency repairs perform well at 96%, above London median of 95%. Non-emergency repairs lag significantly at 66%, 20 points below London median. Total Mobile introduction November 2025 improving visibility; council undertaking work on data quality around work closure dates. Performance gap indicates ongoing operational challenges in repairs delivery.
findings.matters: Significant performance gap versus peer median indicates service quality problem affecting tenant satisfaction and regulatory compliance
findings.figures: Non-emergency 66% on time 2025-26; London median 86%; emergency repairs 96% vs 95% median
findings.quote: In contrast, 66% of non-emergency responsive repairs were completed on time in 2025-26, below the London median of 86%.

findings.paper_title: Lewisham Council Housing Performance Overview 2025-26 REPORT
findings.headline: Disrepair cases account for 36% of repair costs in 2025-26, described as placing "huge burden" on HRA and diverting funds from planned investment
findings.detail: Council notes considerable strain on HRA from pressure to invest in stock improvements while maintaining balance amid inflation and new regulations (fire, building safety, Awaab's Law). Disrepair case costs have risen significantly and now account for 36% of overall repair costs in 2025-26, diverting resources from planned and programmed works. Stock condition survey findings not yet fully modeled into HRA, expected to require additional resources.
findings.matters: HRA financial pressure from unplanned disrepair spending constrains capital investment and threatens medium-term debt sustainability
findings.figures: Disrepair at 36% of repair costs in 2025-26, significant increase from prior years; additional investment required for full survey integration
findings.quote: Disrepair is placing a huge burden on the HRA, diverting funds away from planned investment and programmed work, whether delivered by its Direct Labour Organisation and/or contractors.

findings.paper_title: Lewisham Council Housing Performance Overview 2025-26 REPORT
findings.headline: Repairs work in progress reduced 42% year-on-year to 4,840 jobs
findings.detail: Repairs backlog fell from 8,359 jobs (March 2025) to 4,840 jobs (March 2026), driven by sustained efforts from Direct Labour Organisation and contractors. Of remaining jobs, 28% allocated to contractors and 72% to DLO. Total Mobile system introduced November 2025 improved visibility and control. Data cleansing increased confidence that remaining jobs reflect true outstanding work.
findings.matters: Significant operational progress on a major improvement area supports recovery narrative and addresses self-referral concern
findings.figures: 4,840 jobs March 2026 vs 8,359 March 2025 (42% reduction); 28% contractor allocation, 72% DLO
findings.quote: As at March 2026, repairs work in progress (WIP) stood at 4,840 jobs, representing a significant reduction from 8,359 jobs in March 2025.

findings.paper_title: Lewisham Council Housing Performance Overview 2025-26 REPORT
findings.headline: Fire remedial actions backlog stalled at 2,466 overdue, ending momentum from prior year reduction
findings.detail: Backlog had reduced from over 5,000 at self-referral to 2,248 by end 2024-25. Progress halted during 2025-26 with numbers fluctuating between 2,214-2,494 and ending 2,466 in March 2026. Council confirms zero overdue immediate-risk (P1X) actions as of March 2026, meaning highest-risk fire safety issues addressed. Weekly monitoring in place but further work required for sustained reduction.
findings.matters: Building safety backlog plateau indicates execution risk and signals unresolved regulatory concern from March 2024 self-referral
findings.figures: 2,466 overdue March 2026; down from 5,000+ at self-referral; zero overdue P1X actions
findings.quote: Progress plateaued during 2025-26, with the number of overdue actions fluctuating between 2,214 and 2,494 throughout the year and ending at 2,466 in March 2026.

findings.paper_title: Lewisham Council Housing Performance Overview 2025-26 REPORT
findings.headline: Decent Homes Standard at 15.1% overall, exceeding council's target of 10% by March 2026
findings.detail: Overall non-decent homes improved from 17.4% in 2024-25 to 15.1% in 2025-26, representing material progress. However, this exceeded the council's March 2026 target of 10%. Performance reached approximately 12% in January 2026 but was affected by delays to major works programmes. The majority of failures are due to key building components reaching end of lifespan, outpacing replacement programmes.
findings.matters: Missing the Decent Homes target indicates slower execution than planned on a key regulatory issue from the March 2024 self-referral
findings.figures: 15.1% in 2025-26 vs 10% target; improved from 17.4% in 2024-25; represents 1,804 non-decent properties
findings.quote: the proportion of homes that do not meet the Decent Homes Standard reduced from 17.4% in 2024-25 to 15.1% in 2025-26. While this represents positive progress, it is above the council's target of 10% by March 2026.

findings.paper_title: Lewisham Council Housing Performance Overview 2025-26 REPORT
findings.headline: Comprehensive stock survey found 26% of council-managed homes non-decent, higher than prior estimates
findings.detail: Prior estimates were based on a partial 2019 survey with extrapolated data. A comprehensive stock condition survey by Savills in early 2025 revealed 26% of council-managed homes non-decent. This higher-than-expected finding indicates substantially greater capital investment needs than previously modeled. Subsequent reduction to 16.1% by 2025-26 through targeted investment shows progress but starting point created significant HRA implications.
findings.matters: The survey revealed much larger than previously understood stock quality issues, increasing capital investment needs and HRA financial pressure
findings.figures: 26% of council-managed homes non-decent at survey; prior estimate ~17% based on 2019 partial survey; improved to 16.1% by 2025-26
findings.quote: The survey found that 26% of council-managed homes did not meet the Decent Homes Standard.

findings.paper_title: Lewisham Council Housing Performance Overview 2025-26 REPORT
findings.headline: Council subject to Regulatory Notice from Regulator of Social Housing issued March 2024
findings.detail: The council self-referred to the Regulator in December 2023 regarding homes not meeting Decent Homes Standard, overdue fire remedial actions, and works in progress in Repairs Service. A regulatory notice was served in March 2024, and the council has been meeting monthly with the Regulator to provide progress updates on its Housing Improvement Plan.
findings.matters: Regulatory action signals governance failure and control issues, creating credit and reputational risk for lenders
findings.figures: Issued March 2024; monthly regulator engagement ongoing
findings.quote: Mayor and Cabinet should note that the council remains subject to a Regulatory Notice issued by the Regulator of Social Housing in March 2024.

findings.paper_title: Financial Monitoring 2026-27 – Period 4 Monitoring Appendix
findings.headline: Nightly paid temporary accommodation fell to 869 in July 2026, down from 1,512 in August 2024, a 43% reduction
findings.detail: Monitoring data shows the number of people in nightly paid temporary accommodation has declined substantially from a peak of 1,512 in August 2024 to 869 by July 2026, a reduction of 643 people. This 43% decrease in the homelessness caseload is significant for spending control, as temporary accommodation is high-cost. The related £2.49m Temporary Accommodation Cost Reduction saving is marked Green for delivery, and the reduced caseload demonstrates that this saving should be achievable.
findings.matters: Temporary accommodation is expensive; declining numbers free up budget headroom and reduce a service where spending can spiral; this is one of the few demand trends shown moving in a cost-reducing direction, supporting budget recovery.
findings.figures: 1,512 (August 2024 peak), 869 (July 2026), 643-person reduction (42.5%); £2.49m Temporary Accommodation Cost Reduction saving (Green status)
findings.quote: the level has increased from 1214 in April 2024 to a high of 1512 in August 2024, this has now reduced to 869 in July 2026.

findings.paper_title: Financial Monitoring 2026-27 – Period 4 Monitoring Appendix
findings.headline: Children with Education, Health Care Plans showing sustained upward trend across 2024-25, 2025-26, and 2026-27
findings.detail: The monitoring dashboard includes a graph tracking EHCP numbers across three financial years. The visual shows the 2024-25 baseline line, the 2025-26 line positioned above it, and the 2026-27 line tracking above both prior years, indicating continued year-on-year growth. The graph shows numbers ranging from approximately 3,300 to 4,100 across the three-year period.
findings.matters: EHCP numbers drive significant and growing education, health, and social care spending; councils must forecast these costs over multiple years; sustained upward trends signal structural service pressures.
findings.figures: Approximately 3,300–4,100 range across three financial years with year-on-year increases visible
findings.quote: Children with Education, Health Care Plans

findings.paper_title: Financial Monitoring 2026-27 – Period 4 Monitoring Appendix
findings.headline: Adult social care demand increased to 4,088 people supported by July 2026, up from 3,969 in April, a 3% rise in three months
findings.detail: Monitoring data shows the number of adults receiving social care rising from 3,969 in April to 4,088 in July, an increase of 119 people. This 3% growth in demand occurs against a backdrop of two major social care cost-control savings marked as at-risk: a £2.00m saving on Prevention & Technology improvements (Red) and a £0.50m saving from review of high-cost care home placements (Amber). Rising demand without achieved cost controls amplifies budget pressure.
findings.matters: Adult social care is a budget-critical service with structural demand growth; finance directors and lenders monitor demand trends closely, especially when planned cost controls are not materializing.
findings.figures: 4,088 (July), 3,969 (April), +119 people, +3% over three months
findings.quote: This graph shows the number of adults supported from 24/25 onwards. The source data is the Controcc System.

findings.paper_title: Financial Monitoring 2026-27 – Period 4 Monitoring Appendix
findings.headline: Placement Sufficiency Cost Saving £6.29m marked Red; Adult Social Care Prevention & Technology £2.00m and other Red items total £9.19m
findings.detail: The 2026-27 budget savings plan includes multiple items marked Red (not on track) or Amber (at risk). The largest single Red item is Placement Sufficiency Cost Saving at £6.29m. Other Red-status items include Adult Social Care Prevention & Technology (£2.00m), Home School Transport (£0.40m), and Parking Contract (£0.50m). Amber items include Target Operating Model Review (£1.60m) and Care Home Placements review (£0.50m). Combined Red items total £9.19m, Amber items total £2.10m.
findings.matters: Local authorities must deliver planned savings to balance budgets; this level of at-risk savings—approximately 37% of the total plan—represents a significant threat to the 2026-27 financial position.
findings.figures: £6.29m (Placement Sufficiency), £2.00m (Adult Social Care Prevention), £1.60m (Target Operating Model Review), £0.50m (two items), £0.40m (Home School Transport); total Red £9.19m, total Amber £2.10m
findings.quote: Placement Sufficiency Cost Saving 6.29Red

findings.paper_title: Developing a Community-Led Housing Partnership Strategy REPORT v2
findings.headline: Council states financial constraints have made transfer of council land at below-market or nil value increasingly difficult; introduces 50% social rent threshold for land subsidies.
findings.detail: Council explicitly states it is 'operating within a challenging financial environment' which has made 'the Council's ability to support Community-Led Housing organisations through the transfer of land at below-market or nil value has become increasingly constrained'. However, it remains 'prepared to consider the transfer of land at below-market or nil value where a scheme can demonstrate a proportion of social rent delivery, at 50% or higher assessed against the social value generated', signalling a shift from unconditional land subsidy to conditional support tied to social outcomes.
findings.matters: Shows how financial constraints are reshaping council affordable housing policy and signals to lenders and peers how councils are tightening discretionary spending on asset transfers while maintaining strategic housing commitments.
findings.figures: 50% or higher social rent threshold for land transfers
findings.quote: Like many local authorities, the Council is operating within a challenging financial environment and must ensure that the use and disposal of public assets delivers the greatest possible benefit for residents. The Council's ability to support Community-Led Housing organisations through the transfer of land at below-market or nil value has become increasingly constrained

findings.paper_title: Lewisham Town Centre Improvement Programme – Programme and Budget Update PART 1
findings.headline: Capital contingency allocation reduced from £10m to £3.2m after £4.4m drawdown for Town Centre and £1m commitment for Catford within four months
findings.detail: Full Council approved a £10m capital contingency allocation in July 2026 across General Fund and Housing Revenue Account budgets, funded from reserves. This report proposes to utilise £4.4m for the Town Centre Improvement Programme. An additional £1m capital budget was committed to the Catford Business Plan in September 2026. This leaves approximately £3.2m of the original £10m contingency remaining available.
findings.matters: Material drawdown of the capital contingency within four months reduces the council's financial flexibility for managing unforeseen events or capital pressures elsewhere. The remaining £3.2m headroom is modest relative to the council's overall capital programme exposure.
findings.figures: Total approved contingency July 2026: £10,000,000; Town Centre allocation: £4,403,053.70; Catford allocation September 2026: £1,000,000; remaining balance: approximately £3,200,000
findings.quote: This report is proposing to utilise £4.4m of this, which is in addition to the recent Catford Business Plan request in September which had agreement for £1.4m of revenue and £1m of capital budget, meaning that £3.2m will remain available.

findings.paper_title: Lewisham Town Centre Improvement Programme – Programme and Budget Update PART 1
findings.headline: Blue Garage Ltd awarded Library Operator concession contract for £10.7m over 10 years; operator income forecast £3.6m
findings.detail: Blue Garage Ltd selected after competitive procurement (two bids received, one failed quality threshold). The concession contract provides an initial 5-year term with council option to extend for further 5 years. Estimated contract value comprises £3.6m potential operator income plus £1.75m council fees over the initial 5-year period, totalling £5.35m per 5 years or £10.7m if fully extended. The original Mayor and Cabinet approval in September 2025 did not fully account for the concession value and VAT, necessitating this report to obtain approval of the correct contract value.
findings.matters: The concession model places operating revenue risk on the council. The operator must generate the forecasted £3.6m income or council's library service budget will be impacted. This contract structure is unusual for local government and requires effective performance management.
findings.figures: Estimated concession contract value 10 years £10,704,000; estimated operator income 5 years £3,600,000; estimated council fees 5 years £1,752,000
findings.quote: Approve the award of the Lewisham Library Operator concession contract to Blue Garage Ltd for a period of five years with the option to extend for up to a further 5 years at a value of £10,704,000 over the full contract period.

findings.paper_title: Lewisham Town Centre Improvement Programme – Programme and Budget Update PART 1
findings.headline: Programme completion funded through borrowing-backed capital headroom, carrying borrowing-cost and revenue implications not yet quantified in Part 1
findings.detail: The proposed funding route relies on borrowing to bridge the £4.5m additional requirement. The paper acknowledges this will carry borrowing-cost and revenue implications affecting the council's medium-term budget, but these financial impacts are not quantified in this Part 1 report.
findings.matters: Borrowing creates ongoing revenue budget impacts through interest and financing charges. The unquantified cost and the reduction in future capital flexibility are material considerations for the council's financial position.
findings.figures: Implied borrowing requirement approximately £4.5m; interest cost not quantified
findings.quote: The proposed funding route will rely on borrowing-backed capital headroom and will therefore carry borrowing-cost and revenue implications.

findings.paper_title: Lewisham Town Centre Improvement Programme – Programme and Budget Update PART 1
findings.headline: Market Canopy open procurement returned no compliant bids; FM Conway contract variation approved at £2.9m against original £1.6m design envelope
findings.detail: An open market procurement undertaken in 2025 received three tenders but none met the council's required quality threshold and submissions performed poorly on social value assessment. The council developed an alternative delivery route through FM Conway, its existing Highways Term Contractor, with Mayor and Cabinet approving a £2.9m contract variation in February 2026. This represents a £1.3m increase in this programme element alone compared to the original design procurement envelope of approximately £1.6m.
findings.matters: Procurement challenges forced a shift from open market competition to existing contractor arrangement. This element alone demonstrates the scale of construction cost pressure affecting the wider programme independent of the later Library discoveries.
findings.figures: Original procurement envelope approximately £1.6m; FM Conway approved variation £2.9m; increase £1.3m
findings.quote: Officers developed a delivery route through the Council's existing Highways Term Contractor, FM Conway, and Mayor and Cabinet approved a contract variation of £2.9m for that work in February 2026.

findings.paper_title: Lewisham Town Centre Improvement Programme – Programme and Budget Update PART 1
findings.headline: Library refurbishment discovered extensive concealed structural and building-fabric defects during construction, extending programme by almost a year
findings.detail: Rooff Construction commenced work on-site in September 2025. Opening-up of the building exposed significant defects including untied and unsafe brickwork requiring replacement with steel structures, corroded concrete reinforcement with exposed rebar, defective floor and roof structures, unsafe plantroom structure requiring demolition and replacement, and extensive additional fire safety works. The remedial works will extend the construction period by almost a year. Main Library construction is now forecast to complete summer 2027 with reopening in autumn 2027. Project reporting indicates positive contractor performance.
findings.matters: Hidden condition defects discovered in construction represent significant project delivery risk. The building was known to be complex pre-tender, but the extent of concealed structural and fabric issues could only be confirmed through intrusive opening-up works.
findings.figures: Original estimate approximately £5.4m; tender award £6,532,085; programme extension almost 12 months
findings.quote: Opening-up of the building then exposed further structural and building-fabric defects requiring significant remedial work and an extension of the construction programme.

findings.paper_title: Lewisham Town Centre Improvement Programme – Programme and Budget Update PART 1
findings.headline: Lewisham Town Centre Improvement Programme funding requirement increased by £4.5m to £30.5m; £4.4m funded from capital contingency with remainder dependent on uncertain asset sale receipt
findings.detail: The programme's original budget was approximately £24m (£19m government grant plus £5m council match). The current additional requirement of £4.5m is being funded through an increased capital receipt estimate (£103k), drawing £4.4m from the capital contingency allocation approved in July 2026, and sale of site materials (£24k). The Library Resource Centre sale is estimated at £1.3m but is flagged as at-risk, with potential for receipts to be higher or lower. The updated total programme budget is now £30,488,326.
findings.matters: A 27% increase in programme cost is material and impacts the council's financial capacity and future capital planning. The funding route relies heavily on capital reserves and an uncertain asset sale, reducing flexibility for other capital priorities.
findings.figures: Original budget approximately £24m; additional requirement £4.5m; updated budget £30,488,326.00; contingency allocation £4,403,053.70; Library Resource Centre sale estimate £1,300,000
findings.quote: The current working additional funding requirement to complete LTCIP is around £4.5m, subject to final Finance reconciliation.

findings.paper_title: Housing Major Works Procurement Strategy REPORT
findings.headline: Strategy intended to improve value for money through competition and benchmarking; savings have not been quantified and no saving assumption built into HRA business plan
findings.detail: The strategy aims to improve value for money through competition, benchmarking, whole-life cost assessment and independent cost assurance. However, savings have not been quantified at this stage and no assumption of saving has been built into the HRA business plan. This is noted explicitly in financial implications.
findings.matters: For a £350m five-year programme, the expected value improvements and cost benefits of the procurement investment have not been quantified
findings.figures: £350m over five years to 2031; £70m annual programme
findings.quote: Savings have not been quantified at this stage and no assumption of saving has been built into the HRA business plan.

findings.paper_title: Housing Major Works Procurement Strategy REPORT
findings.headline: Framework vehicle choice determines whether procurement and management costs fall to HRA revenue or are capitalised through capital programme
findings.detail: A Lewisham-led framework carries procurement, legal and management costs that may fall to HRA revenue budgets. An external framework charges fees as a percentage of call-off value, potentially capitalisable. The options appraisal will compare total costs and relative HRA revenue and capital impacts of each option before authority to procure.
findings.matters: Framework choice affects both HRA revenue budget pressure and capital programme affordability in ways not yet quantified
findings.figures: External framework fees typically charged as percentage of call-off value
findings.quote: External framework fees are generally recovered through project expenditure and may therefore be capable of being capitalised as part of the cost of delivering works, whereas the procurement, legal and management costs associated with establishing a Lewisham-led framework may fall to HRA revenue budgets.

findings.paper_title: Housing Major Works Procurement Strategy REPORT
findings.headline: Additional client-side programme and contract-management capacity required; cost and HRA funding source to be quantified before authority to procure
findings.detail: A broader supplier base and stronger assurance model require additional client-side programme, commercial, technical and contract-management capacity. The council is explicitly told that the benefits in this report are not deliverable without that investment. The requirement will be quantified through a client capacity assessment before authority to procure.
findings.matters: Strategy cannot be delivered without resource investment whose scale, cost and HRA budget impact are not yet known
findings.figures: None provided
findings.quote: Mayor and Cabinet is asked to note that the benefits set out in this report are not deliverable without that investment.

findings.paper_title: Housing Major Works Procurement Strategy REPORT
findings.headline: New general major works arrangement must be mobilised by April 2028, well before existing contracts expire August 2029
findings.detail: The critical path requires authority to procure by April 2027, main competition during 2027, and mobilisation by April 2028—approximately 16 months before current contracts expire. The paper identifies procurement timetable slippage as a key risk, with escalation to Executive Management Team if mobilisation date is at risk.
findings.matters: Missing the April 2028 mobilisation target would leave only months before existing contracts expire, risking programme continuity and triggering contingency procurement costs
findings.figures: April 2028 required mobilisation; August 2029 contract expiry
findings.quote: The critical path is to obtain authority to procure by April 2027, complete the main competition during 2027 and mobilise the future general major works arrangement by April 2028, well before the current contracts expire in August 2029.

findings.paper_title: Housing Major Works Procurement Strategy REPORT
findings.headline: Independent reviews of major works schemes commissioned to examine scope and value for money; leaseholders have complained that estimated costs do not represent good value
findings.detail: The previous extension report identified programming gaps, variable delivery outcomes, and inconsistent contractor readiness. The council has commissioned independent reviews examining scope and value for money; findings are awaited. Leaseholders have separately complained that estimated costs from existing contracts do not represent good value.
findings.matters: Affordability and value-for-money concerns affect both operational performance and leaseholder service charge recovery, which are material to HRA revenue sustainability
findings.figures: £127m delivered by both contractors since 2021; reviews outcome awaited
findings.quote: There have also been leaseholder complaints that the estimated cost of works derived from the contracts do not represent good value.

findings.paper_title: Housing Major Works Procurement Strategy REPORT
findings.headline: Both measured term contracts can be terminated by either party with six months' notice; neither contract guarantees any volume of work
findings.detail: The council currently depends on United Infrastructure and Mulalley measured term contracts for major works. Both extend to August 2029 but carry no-fault break clauses exercisable by either party on six months' notice. The council is explicitly directed not to plan on the basis that both contracts will still be in place in 2029, creating immediate operational vulnerability.
findings.matters: For a £330m HRA capital programme over five years, unplanned loss of either contractor would create immediate delivery risk and require emergency replacement procurement
findings.figures: £70m annual programme; £330m HRA capital over five years to 2031; six months' termination notice; August 2029 expiry
findings.quote: Both MTCs carry a no-fault break provision on six months' notice, exercisable by either party, and neither guarantees any volume of work. The Council should therefore not plan on the basis that both contracts will run to August 2029.

findings.paper_title: Financial Monitoring 2026-27 – Period 4 Monitoring REPORT
findings.headline: Business Rates collected at 103% of 99% budgeted collection target as at 31 July
findings.detail: Business rates collection running ahead of target at 103% vs 99% budgeted collection rate. Collection described as 'higher than expected for this time of the year' due to school transfers of funds for payment. This represents positive performance in at least one revenue stream, offsetting council tax collection weakness.
findings.matters: Provides partial offset to council tax collection shortfall; shows resilience in at least one key revenue stream; demonstrates collection capability where economic conditions permit
findings.figures: 103% collection rate vs 99% target, £31.6m collected against £30.7m billed
findings.quote: £31.6m of business rates due had been collected which is a 103% collection rate, however, there is a budgeted 99% collection target

findings.paper_title: Financial Monitoring 2026-27 – Period 4 Monitoring REPORT
findings.headline: Capital programme financing plan includes £294.1m prudential borrowing across MTFS period (£51.5m General Fund, £242.6m HRA)
findings.detail: Total capital programme £776.8m over MTFS period. 2026-27 allocation £244.0m with £36.0m (15%) spent to date by 31 July 2026. Prudential borrowing represents significant debt load across medium term. Financing also dependent on capital receipts, grants, and reserves. Some slippage evident: Strategic Regeneration Catford programme reduced from £2.2m budget to £0.7m forecast; some HRA projects under review. Revenue costs of financing will be material and dependent on interest rate environment.
findings.matters: Lenders need sight of total debt trajectory and affordability; HRA borrowing particularly material relative to declining reserves position; capital slippage affects treasury management and revenue cost management; interest rate risk on unfinanced borrowing
findings.figures: £294.1m prudential borrowing (£51.5m GF, £242.6m HRA), £776.8m total capital programme, £244.0m 2026-27 allocation, £36.0m spent (15%)
findings.quote: Total Prudential Borrowing of £294.1m across the MTFS period, of which £51.5m is for GF projects & £242.6m is for HRA projects.

findings.paper_title: Financial Monitoring 2026-27 – Period 4 Monitoring REPORT
findings.headline: Children's and Adult Social Care both forecasting £4.2m overspends driven by volume growth in placements, with £6.29m placement sufficiency saving rated Red
findings.detail: Children's Services: shift from in-house to external fostering agencies creating cost pressure; over-18s placement costs rising at rates higher than rest of London (no equivalent robust review has been conducted on over-18s as was done for under-18s); placement sufficiency saving of £6.29m is rated Red. Adult Social Care: forecast allows 'no headroom for additional growth'; packages and placements commitment increased £5.1m between 2025-26 outturn and current forecast; very high demand on hospital discharge pathway. Both services implementing oversight panels and cost management actions including recruitment restrictions, reablement focus, and AI assessment tools.
findings.matters: Structural demand pressures in statutory services (Children Act and Care Act); no contingency for volume growth means any further increase will blow budget; cost management actions (panel oversight, recruitment restrictions) may impact service timeliness and quality; risks extend through year
findings.figures: Children's £4.2m overspend (Family Help & Care £4.7m), Adult Social Care £4.2m overspend, £5.1m increase in packages/placements, £6.29m placement sufficiency saving rated Red
findings.quote: There is an increase in those in external fostering agencies and reduction using in-house fostering which is causing a cost pressure. There is also an increase in costs related to those receiving care over 18 years old.

findings.paper_title: Financial Monitoring 2026-27 – Period 4 Monitoring REPORT
findings.headline: Parking Services contract delivering £1.3m overspend with additional £1.0m disputed claim from contractor Marston's for prior-year costs
findings.detail: Contract costs higher than anticipated. Contractor has claimed £1.0m for costs in previous financial year; claim rejected by council but contractor asserts debt remains outstanding and dispute is ongoing. Additional concern identified about ambiguity in debt management by contractor and whether council is assured it is receiving all income due.
findings.matters: Significant contract underperformance suggests either contract management weakness or unforeseen cost drivers; disputed liability creates contingent cash flow risk; wider debt collection assurance issue
findings.figures: £1.3m overspend, £1.0m disputed claim
findings.quote: The parking contractors, are claiming for costs of c£1m which were incurred in the previous financial year. These costs have been rejected, however, the company have stated that they believe that the debt is still outstanding.

findings.paper_title: Financial Monitoring 2026-27 – Period 4 Monitoring REPORT
findings.headline: HRA closing reserves forecast at £14.0m, down from opening £45.9m, leaving only 'slightly above 10% recommended balance'
findings.detail: HRA reserves will be depleted by £31.9m through the year. £2.3m overspend combined with £25.0m planned revenue contribution to capital programme is driving drawdown (offset by capital financing transactions). findings.paper_title: Approval to Extend the Council’s Insurances REPORT
findings.headline: Market conditions make new insurance procurement unlikely to achieve materially better pricing or terms than existing arrangements.
findings.detail: The council's appointed insurance brokers assessed market conditions and concluded that undertaking new procurement would not deliver better terms than the current arrangements. The public sector insurance market is served by a limited number of insurers, all experiencing inflationary and cost pressures. The council has decided to extend existing arrangements that have performed satisfactorily since 2023, maintaining relationship continuity and avoiding procurement costs.
findings.matters: Other councils considering whether to re-tender insurance arrangements need to understand whether competitive processes offer advantage in the current market environment.
findings.figures: Eight insurance lots covering all major classes; three-year initial contract from December 2023, now extended through November 2028.
findings.quote: market intelligence obtained through the Council's insurance brokers indicates that undertaking a new procurement exercise is unlikely to deliver materially better pricing or terms than those available under the existing arrangements.

findings.paper_title: Approval to Extend the Council’s Insurances REPORT
findings.headline: Insurance premiums have increased approximately 6% annually from 2023-2025, with similar increases expected during the 2026-2028 extension period.
findings.detail: Insurance costs rose from £2,392,171 in 2023 to £2,672,094 in 2025, representing roughly 6% annual increases. An indicative 6% increase from December 2026 would bring costs to £2,832,420 for the first year of extension. The two-year extension is budgeted at £5.8m. These increases reflect market-wide pressures affecting all public sector insurers, including inflation, litigation costs, property repair costs, and reinsurance expenses.
findings.matters: Finance directors need to understand fixed cost pressures that cannot be reduced through procurement due to universal market conditions, showing budget constraints extend even to unavoidable expenses.

findings.paper_title: Treasury Management Outturn and Mid-Year Review 2026-27 Council
findings.headline: Investment reserves declining from £264m to £210m as council depletes cash to fund capital, reducing financial flexibility.
findings.detail: The council's liquid investment portfolio has shrunk by £54m from £264m (June 2025) to £210m (June 2026), and the yield has fallen from 4.3% to 3.7%. The council is deliberately running down these reserves as an alternative to borrowing for capital spend, but this strategy is being exhausted. As cash reserves deplete, the council will become increasingly reliant on capital markets borrowing. The document indicates investment returns will continue to fall as interest rates are expected to decline.
findings.matters: Declining cash reserves indicate the council is exhausting alternative funding options and will become entirely dependent on borrowed funding once reserves are depleted, removing its financial buffer and making it more vulnerable to adverse borrowing conditions or unexpected cost pressures.
findings.figures: Investments: £264m (June 2025) → £210m (June 2026), a decline of £54m; yield declining from 4.3% to 3.7%.
findings.quote: The current investments of £210m as at 30 June 2026 (£264m 2025) will give the Council a 3.7% return compared to 4.3% at June 2025.

findings.paper_title: Treasury Management Outturn and Mid-Year Review 2026-27 Council
findings.headline: LOBO loans reduced by £65m in two years (£119.7m to £54.3m), with further £17.5m repaid since April 2026, reducing refinancing risk.
findings.detail: The council has systematically reduced its LOBO (Lender's Option Borrower's Option) exposure from £119.7m to £54.3m over two years, plus an additional £17.5m repayment since April 2026. This brings the outstanding balance to approximately £36.8m. The council had been in correspondence with its LOBO lenders exploring rescheduling opportunities. This proactive reduction removes exposure to refinancing risk if lenders exercise their call option at higher rates.
findings.matters: LOBOs create refinancing risk at call dates; if exercised, the council must choose between repaying at par or accepting a new (potentially higher) rate. Reducing this exposure demonstrates sound risk management and reduces financial volatility from refinancing decisions outside the council's control.
findings.figures: LOBO loans: £119.7m (two years ago) → £54.3m (31 March 2026) → approximately £36.8m (post-April 2026); total reduction of £83m over two years.
findings.quote: In the last two years the Council has reduced its LOBO loans from £119.7m to £54.3m as at 31 March 2026. Since 1 April 2026 the Council has repaid a further £17.5m of LOBO loans.

findings.paper_title: Treasury Management Outturn and Mid-Year Review 2026-27 Council

This rising trend means an increasing share of the council's annual budget is locked into servicing debt, leaving less flexibility for service delivery and less resilience to unexpected pressures.
findings.matters: A rising debt service ratio indicates increasing financial stress and eroding budget flexibility. Lenders track this closely as an indicator of whether the council can sustain its debt burden without compromising service delivery or requiring spending cuts.
findings.figures: Financing costs as percentage of net revenue (excl. PFI): 4.8% (2025/26 actual), 6.0% (2026/27 estimate), 7.7% (2027/28 estimate).

findings.paper_title: Treasury Management Outturn and Mid-Year Review 2026-27 Council
findings.headline: Capital programme jumped 62% in three months from £421.4m to £684.6m, forcing substantial new borrowing (£72.6m in 2026/27 alone).
findings.detail: Between March and June 2026, Lewisham's four-year capital programme forecast increased by £263.2m — a 62% rise. This forces the council to shift from its under-borrowing strategy to active borrowing. The council will need £42m general fund borrowing and £30.6m HRA borrowing in 2026/27. The bulk of the increase comes from the Housing Revenue Account, particularly the 'Building for Lewisham' programme.
findings.matters: A lender would need to understand what is driving such a large and rapid increase in capital plans, whether this reflects a sustained policy shift, and how sustainable the resulting additional borrowing will be for the council's medium-term finances.
findings.figures: Capital programme: £421.4m (March 2026 forecast) to £684.6m (June 2026 forecast); prudential borrowing requirement: £42.0m general fund and £30.6m HRA for 2026/27.
findings.quote: The Capital Programme for 2026-30 was agreed as £421.4m in March 2026 and is now forecast to be £684.6m as at 30 June 2026, an increase of £263.2m.

findings.matters: A lender needs confidence in financial projections; a council acknowledging that its rate forecast is likely to be revised upward within weeks suggests significant uncertainty about 2026-27 borrowing costs and the stability of treasury assumptions
findings.figures: Forecast made June 2026; Middle East conflict broke out after June; revision expected due to inflation
findings.quote: We expect MUFG to provide a revised forecast as pressure on inflation grows.

findings.detail: MUFG's borrowing advice states that all PWLB certainty rates are currently significantly above the neutral 3.5% Bank Rate level. MUFG advises better value can be obtained at the shorter end of the curve and short-dated fixed Local Authority to Local Authority monies should be considered, rather than longer-maturity borrowing.
findings.matters: The advisor is flagging that long-term borrowing is currently expensive relative to long-term neutral levels; councils considering capital expenditure will face higher costs if borrowing long-term
findings.figures: MUFG neutral Bank Rate forecast 3.5% (long-term); all PWLB certainty rates currently significantly above this level
findings.quote: Overall, better value can be obtained at the shorter end of the curve and short-dated fixed LA to LA monies should also be considered.

findings.paper_title: Treasury Management Strategy 2026-27 Appendices - Final
findings.headline: UK inflation remains stubborn with risk of breaching 4.5%, driving expectations of higher debt interest costs
findings.detail: UK inflation peaked at 3.8% then dipped to 3% in January-February before core inflation rose to 3.2% in February. The document warns that recent upward pressure on energy costs could see CPI inflation breach 4.5% later in 2026. This inflation backdrop is expected to increase government debt interest repayments by approximately £10bn.
findings.matters: Rising inflation increases the cost to a council of servicing existing and new debt, and indicates a risk that council spending pressures (utilities, energy costs) will also rise
findings.figures: CPI peaked at 3.8%, dipped to 3%, core inflation 3.2% in February; risk of breaching 4.5% later in year; government debt interest repayment increase of £10bn
findings.quote: the recent upward pressure on energy costs could see CPI inflation breach 4.5% later this year.

findings.paper_title: Treasury Management Strategy 2026-27 Appendices - Final
findings.headline: Interest rate forecast shifted to expect Bank Rate will remain at 3.75% or rise, not fall, as inflation pressures increase
findings.detail: MUFG Corporate Markets now expects the MPC will not cut Bank Rate and may even raise rates due to inflation driven by the war in the Middle East. The forecast was made in June 2026 before the ceasefire was broken. This represents a shift from earlier expectations of rate cuts. The PWLB borrowing rates forecast shows 5-year rates at 4.30% in September 2026, 10-year at 4.90%, and 25-year at 5.60%.
findings.matters: If Bank Rate remains at 3.75% or rises rather than falls, councils face higher borrowing costs for 2026-27; this affects both the cost of any new borrowing and the calculus on refinancing existing debt
findings.figures: Bank Rate forecast 3.75% (Sep 2026-Sep 2027); PWLB rates 5-year 4.30%, 10-year 4.90%, 25-year 5.60%
findings.quote: MUFG Corporate Markets now expect the MPC will not cut Bank Rate and may even raise rates as inflation increases due to the war in the Middle East.

findings.paper_title: 5a. Treasury Management Outturn and Mid Year Review 202627
findings.headline: Net borrowing requirement for 2025/26 was £9.7m, down from £60.8m in 2024/25
findings.detail: The net borrowing requirement fell significantly year-on-year from £60.8m to £9.7m, a reduction of £51.1m or 84%. This improvement reflects lower capital investment in the year (£137.1m vs £159.3m), higher capital grants received (£47.5m), increased capital receipts (£6.2m), and revenue contributions to capital expenditure (£18.6m). However, forward projections indicate this improvement will reverse due to the capital programme expansion and higher borrowing needs in 2026/27 and beyond.
findings.matters: Shows the underlying improvement in borrowing pressures for 2025/26; context for understanding that forward trajectory is now moving sharply higher.

findings.paper_title: 5a. Treasury Management Outturn and Mid Year Review 202627
findings.headline: Internal borrowing increased to £345.4m as at 31 March 2026 from £328.8m previous year
findings.detail: The council is maintaining an under-borrowed position, using reserves and cash balances to fund £345.4m of its £689.3m capital financing requirement, with the remainder (£343.9m) funded by external debt. This strategy is pursued while investment returns (3.7%) remain lower than borrowing costs. As the capital programme expands and investment balances decline, this internal borrowing gap is forecast to widen, requiring eventual recourse to external borrowing.
findings.matters: Shows the council's capital financing strategy and cash position; the growing gap between capital financing requirement and external debt signals increasing dependence on cash reserves as investments are drawn down.

findings.paper_title: 5a. Treasury Management Outturn and Mid Year Review 202627
findings.headline: LOBO loans reduced from £119.7m to £54.3m over two years, with further £17.5m repaid in April-June 2026
findings.detail: The council has aggressively reduced its exposure to LOBO (Lender Option Borrower Option) loans, which carry refinancing risk when lenders exercise call options. From £119.7m two years prior, the portfolio was cut to £54.3m as at 31 March 2026, and an additional £17.5m was repaid between 1 April and 30 June 2026. The council engaged with LOBO lenders during 2024-2025 on rescheduling opportunities and continues to monitor the position if further calls occur.
findings.matters: Demonstrates deliberate action to reduce refinancing risk exposure where lenders hold the option to propose higher rates at call dates; shows active debt portfolio management.
findings.figures: LOBO loans reduced from £119.7m (two years ago) to £54.3m (31 March 2026); additional £17.5m repaid 1 April - 30 June 2026; £65.4m reduction over three-year period

findings.matters: A material expansion in capital plans directly increases the council's underlying borrowing need and sets the scale of treasury and financing decisions for the period ahead.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 4. Catford Regeneration Programme Business Plan v.FINAL
findings.headline: Unfunded ongoing maintenance and enhanced project management capacity identified as necessary for delivery success, adding to capital and revenue funding pressures
findings.detail: Beyond capital gaps, the business plan identifies specific revenue pressures: ongoing maintenance costs and 'the need for enhanced programme/project management capacity.' Town centre management activity is mostly funded through existing budgets but 'physical capital works to support crime and ASB prevention are not funded.' The business plan emphasises that 'The resourcing challenges will need to be addressed for the programme to be delivered successfully,' yet identifies no funding source for these requirements.
findings.matters: Unfunded operational costs and management capacity often emerge as revenue pressures post-delivery; their explicit identification but non-funding signals risks to implementation quality and service delivery sustainability.

findings.quote: Revenue pressures associated with project delivery, ongoing maintenance and the need for enhanced programme/project management capacity. The resourcing challenges will need to be addressed for the programme to be delivered successfully.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 4. Catford Regeneration Programme Business Plan v.FINAL
findings.headline: Regeneration programme faces 'insufficient capital and revenue budgets' with identified funding gaps for High Street Place Lab and limited contingency allowances
findings.detail: The business plan explicitly states there is 'insufficient capital and revenue budgets available to deliver the entirety of the programme.' Capital funding gaps are specifically identified for the High Street Place Lab programme. Even where funding is secured for core transport projects, 'contingency allowances remain limited and aspects of the programme may need to be refined to remain within budget.' findings.matters: Explicit acknowledgment of insufficient budgets across a major regeneration programme signals either undelivered projects or potential unplanned calls on council reserves or borrowing.

Council has built consultation into its procurement timeline (Oct 2026 and Feb 2027).
findings.matters: Leaseholder charges are a material HRA income stream; failure to follow proper consultation process could significantly reduce budgeted cost recovery and create unplanned financial pressure on HRA

findings.paper_title: Approval to enact permitted extension to 0-19 Public Health Nursing Service contract - Report
findings.headline: Service has undergone prior £350,000 reduction in 2021/22 and now spends less per capita than most comparable Inner London boroughs, despite serving a higher-deprivation population.
findings.detail: The service was subject to a £350,000 budget cut in 2021/22, which became the budget base for re-commissioning in 2022/23. Current per capita spend on 0-19 Public Health Nursing is moderate across all London boroughs, but when compared with Inner London boroughs only, Lewisham spends less per capita than most other areas. This is notable given that Lewisham has relatively high deprivation levels compared to other London boroughs. Efficiencies have been achieved through increased skill-mix and management restructuring.
findings.matters: Shows council has limited scope for further efficiency savings in this service; relevant for understanding constraints on spending and whether current service levels are sustainable relative to deprivation need.
findings.quote: A £350,000 cut was made to the contact value in the 2021/22 financial year.

findings.paper_title: Approval to enact permitted extension to 0-19 Public Health Nursing Service contract - Report
findings.headline: Funding cliff at 31 March 2029: variations to service (PAIRS and Specialist Nurse roles) end at this date, and core contract continuation depends on annual Public Health Grant allocation.
findings.detail: The Parent-Infant Relationship Services (PAIRS) variation is funded until 31 March 2029, with continuation beyond uncertain. The Specialist School Nurse for Integrated Adolescent Service is similarly funded only until 31 March 2029. The core contract extends to 31 March 2030, but funding comes from annual Public Health Grant allocation, which is subject to government spending decisions. Any uplift to contract value for NHS pay awards must be affordable within available grant allocations.
findings.matters: Creates requirement for council financial planning beyond 2029 to either secure grant continuation, find alternative funding, or plan service reductions; relevant to understanding future financial commitments and risks.
findings.figures: 31 March 2029 (end date for variation services); 31 March 2030 (end date for core contract)
findings.quote: Provision of the grant beyond this point is unknown.

findings.paper_title: Approval to enact permitted extension to 0-19 Public Health Nursing Service contract - Report
findings.headline: Service extension performs better than statistical neighbours and national average on most key performance indicators, supporting decision to extend existing provider rather than procure competitively.
findings.detail: The provider's performance data shows Lewisham Health Visiting Service exceeding statistical neighbours and national averages on most measures: 92% of families receiving new birth visit within 14 days (vs 86% nationally), 90% receiving 6-8 week review (vs 87% nationally), 84% receiving 1-year developmental review (vs 73% statistical neighbours), and 92% of 2-year-olds achieving expected development level (vs 83% nationally). Breastfeeding at 6-8 weeks is 85% vs 57% nationally. Recent commissioning of similar services across London shows minimal competing bids, making a new procurement unlikely to add value.
findings.matters: Demonstrates council is making evidence-based decisions about service continuity; relevant for other councils assessing whether to extend or re-tender established health services.
findings.quote: Based on recent commissioning of Health Visiting and School Nursing Services across London, and the previous commissioning of this contract, it is unlikely that any other NHS Trusts would compete with LGT to bid for the contract.

findings.paper_title: Capital investment to refurbish and operate a 5–6 bed local authority children’s home at 200 Kirkdale, Sydenham - Report

findings.paper_title: Capital investment to refurbish and operate a 5–6 bed local authority children’s home at 200 Kirkdale, Sydenham - Report
findings.headline: Multiple financial assumptions underpinning sinking fund are at risk, potentially accelerating point at which corporate support required.
findings.detail: Model depends on: costs rising by 3% annually; external placement costs at £2.4m per year; occupancy at 90%; void rate at 10%. Report identifies risks: 'If capital or revenue costs rise faster than assumed, if inflation is above the modelled rate, if the children transferred in would otherwise have attracted lower external costs than the current modelling, or if voids exceed the modelled 10% allowance, the reserve will deplete more quickly and the point at which further corporate support is required will move forward.'
findings.matters: Sinking fund model is highly sensitive to cost and utilization variables; deterioration in any assumption could trigger need for corporate support sooner than Year 11, creating additional budget pressure.

findings.paper_title: Capital investment to refurbish and operate a 5–6 bed local authority children’s home at 200 Kirkdale, Sydenham - Report
findings.headline: Financial model indicates further corporate financial support will be required from Year 11 onwards, beyond current modeling period.
findings.detail: The 10-year financial model establishes a sinking fund for capital and lifecycle costs. However the council explicitly states the proposal 'does not remove the need for further corporate financial support in year 11 on the current assumptions.' The report notes that once operational the council will develop a longer-term lifecycle model to budget for costs beyond Year 10.
findings.matters: Proposal creates unquantified long-term financial commitment for the council in future budget cycles; currently unfunded costs will emerge within foreseeable timeframe.
findings.figures: 10-year model period; Year 11+ funding requirement identified but not quantified
findings.quote: does not remove the need for further corporate financial support in year 11 on the current assumptions

findings.paper_title: Capital investment to refurbish and operate a 5–6 bed local authority children’s home at 200 Kirkdale, Sydenham - Report
findings.headline: Financial model depends on placement cost savings but the budget generating those savings is already overspending.
findings.detail: Model assumes £2.4m annual external placement costs versus £1.915m operating costs. Report explicitly states: 'FHC placement budgets are already overspending and therefore... the delivery of the home as modelled does not create net cost savings.' The council must recover an existing overspend in order for the assumed cost avoidance to fund the capital repayment and lifecycle costs.
findings.matters: Capital repayment depends on achieving savings in a budget already in deficit; this creates compounded budget pressure where the council must fix one problem to fund another.
findings.figures: £2.4m annual external placement costs assumed; £1.915m annual Kirkdale running costs; Family Help and Care placement budget currently overspending
findings.quote: FHC placement budgets are already overspending and therefore, while we should be able to fund the capital and lifecycle costs the delivery of the home as modelled does not create net cost savings

findings.headline: Council requires additional £479,000 capital funding beyond previously approved budget to complete Kirkdale refurbishment.

The additional amount is expected to be repaid through placement cost savings achieved in early years of operation. This represents unbudgeted capital addition to a major project.

findings.paper_title: WorkWell – Expanding the health and employment integrated system in Lewisham - Appendix B - WorkWell Section 256-Lewisham and SELICB- V2
findings.headline: WorkWell funding is drawn down quarterly in arrears through quarterly invoicing to ICB
findings.detail: Lewisham will invoice the ICB on a quarterly basis to draw down funding. The ICB submits quarterly claims to DWP 'in arrears.' DWP then verifies and pays the ICB 'on a quarterly basis, in arrears.' This creates a cash flow lag: Lewisham must fund staff payroll and service delivery costs before receiving corresponding income from the ICB.
findings.matters: A finance director must ensure sufficient working capital or reserve capacity to cover quarterly staffing and delivery costs before receiving arrears payments from DWP via the ICB. This is particularly material given the rising participant targets in years 2-3.
findings.figures: Quarterly invoicing and quarterly arrears payment from DWP
findings.quote: The London Borough of Lewisham will invoice the ICB on a quarterly basis to draw down their Work Well funding each quarter... The DWP will verify the claim form and will pay the ICB for the total amount claimed, on a quarterly basis, in arrears.

findings.paper_title: WorkWell – Expanding the health and employment integrated system in Lewisham - Appendix B - WorkWell Section 256-Lewisham and SELICB- V2
findings.headline: SEL ICB must achieve at least 55% of its 890-participant Year 1 target (490 participants) or DWP will take performance management action
findings.detail: The DWP requires the South East London ICB to achieve at least 55% of agreed annual activity targets. If this is not met, 'the DWP will take performance management action.' Lewisham's 171-participant Year 1 target contributes to the collective SEL total, and 'the activity across all six SEL boroughs will be added together to reach this total.' Performance is assessed at ICB level, not by individual borough.
findings.matters: Lewisham's ability to secure continued funding and avoid DWP intervention depends partly on the collective performance of five other councils. If SEL underperforms, it could trigger funding restrictions or conditions affecting Lewisham despite Lewisham's own delivery performance.
findings.figures: 890 total participants required across SEL in Year 1; 55% threshold = 490 participants minimum
findings.quote: DWP require ICB's to achieve at least 55% of their agreed activity target each year, if this is not achieved the DWP will take performance management action.

findings.paper_title: WorkWell – Expanding the health and employment integrated system in Lewisham - Appendix B - WorkWell Section 256-Lewisham and SELICB- V2
findings.headline: Lewisham's WorkWell participation targets grow from 171 participants in Year 1 to 611 in Year 2 and 649 in Year 3
findings.detail: The council must recruit and employ Work and Health Coaches and Multi-Disciplinary Teams to deliver these participants. The Year 2 target is 3.6 times the Year 1 baseline and Year 3 is 3.8 times Year 1. The agreement makes the council 'responsible for the recruitment and employment of staff' to achieve these targets, creating significant staffing cost and recruitment commitments.
findings.matters: The steep growth in participation targets implies substantial payroll and recruitment costs ramping in years 2-3 to deliver a service that is itself conditionally funded. A finance director must plan for staffing and related delivery costs that may exceed available income if DWP does not confirm year 2-3 funding.
findings.figures: Year 1: 171 participants; Year 2: 611 participants; Year 3: 649 participants
findings.quote: WorkWell services are responsible for the recruitment and employment of staff. This must include Work and Health Coaches and Multi-Disciplinary Teams who deliver services

findings.paper_title: WorkWell – Expanding the health and employment integrated system in Lewisham - Appendix B - WorkWell Section 256-Lewisham and SELICB- V2
findings.headline: WorkWell funding for 2027/28 and 2028/29 is indicative and subject to DWP confirmation
findings.detail: Lewisham's Year 1 funding of £193,173 is confirmed, but Years 2 and 3 are explicitly conditional. The agreement states: 'The funding allocations for 2027/28 and 2028/29 are indicative figures and are subject to confirmation of funding from the DWP.' This creates budget planning risk as half the three-year income stream cannot be guaranteed.
findings.matters: A finance director must plan for the possibility that confirmed budget income for years 2-3 does not materialise, forcing reprioritisation of spending or staffing reductions mid-programme.
findings.quote: a further £499,672 in 2027/28 and £541,423 in 2028/29 subject to further confirmation of WorkWell funding allocation to SEL ICB by the Department of Work and Pensions (DWP)

findings.paper_title: 2026-27 Strategic Transport and Highways Capital Programme - Report

findings.matters: Programme funding is not finalized for the full year; a council or lender needs to understand that some capital programmes are contingent on satisfactory progress reporting and could face mid-year increases or reductions.

findings.paper_title: 2026-27 Strategic Transport and Highways Capital Programme - Report

findings.matters: Loss of the incentive element would reduce the highways budget by 17% (£633k of £3.8m), forcing either further reserve draw or programme reduction. The council's ability to retain this funding depends on meeting DfT performance requirements.

findings.quote: £1,637,000 of this is funded through DfT's Local Highway Maintenance Capital Funding 2026-2030, consisting of £1,004,000 baseline and £633,000 incentive funding

findings.paper_title: 2026-27 Strategic Transport and Highways Capital Programme - Report

findings.matters: Material budget risk flagged by the council itself; overrun could trigger either reserve draw-down or new borrowing, both of which affect the council's financial position and debt levels.

findings.paper_title: 2026-27 Strategic Transport and Highways Capital Programme - Report

findings.paper_title: Treasury Management Outturn and Mid-Year Review 2026-27 - Report
findings.headline: Council maintains under-borrowed position of £329m internal borrowing in 2026/27 based on interest rate assumptions
findings.detail: Council continues deliberate strategy of funding capital through cash reserves (internal borrowing) rather than external debt, with forecast internal borrowing of £329m in 2026/27. Strategy is based on assumption that investment returns remain lower than borrowing costs, but this depends on interest rate path.
findings.matters: Shows confidence in interest rate forecasts and ability to manage liquidity; signals vulnerability to rate shock—if borrowing costs fall faster than expected, internal borrowing becomes more expensive than external debt and strategy would reverse.
